questions.q: A 45-year-old patient presents with a pigmented lesion on the back that is clinically suspicious for melanoma. Which biopsy modality is contraindicated and why?
opts: Punch biopsy, because it risks sampling error and cannot assess full Breslow depth
Shave biopsy, because it compromises Breslow depth assessment and cannot evaluate subcutaneous involvement
Incisional biopsy, because it leaves tumor behind requiring a second procedure
Excisional biopsy, because it produces cosmetically unacceptable scarring
questions.exp: Shave and punch biopsies are both contraindicated in suspected melanoma because they fail to provide adequate depth assessment (Breslow thickness) which is critical for staging and prognosis. Excisional biopsy is the gold standard for melanoma as it provides simultaneous diagnosis and definitive treatment with complete margin assessment.

questions.q: A 35-year-old patient with psoriasis presents with elevated antimicrobial peptides in their skin scales. Which of the following AMPs was historically the first to be identified in psoriatic scales and is primarily produced by keratinocytes and sebocytes?
opts: LL-37 (cathelicidin)
Human β-defensin-2 (hBD-2)
Dermcidin (DCD-1)
Calprotectin (S100 protein)
questions.exp: Human β-defensin-2 (hBD-2) was the first AMP discovered in psoriatic scales and remains an important marker of skin immunity. It is produced by keratinocytes and exhibits broad-spectrum antimicrobial activity against bacteria, fungi, and viruses.

questions.q: A 45-year-old man with a long-standing history of multiple schwannomas affecting the spinal cord and peripheral nerves is found to have normal bilateral vestibular systems on audiometric testing and imaging. Genetic testing reveals a mutation in the SMARCB1 gene. Which of the following best distinguishes this patient's condition from classic NF2?
opts: This patient has mosaic NF2 restricted to the spinal and peripheral nervous system
This patient has schwannomatosis, characterized by multiple schwannomas but strictly lacking bilateral vestibular schwannomas
This patient has Gardner-type NF2 with unusually late onset and minimal vestibular involvement
This patient has a postzygotic somatic mutation that will be inherited in an autosomal recessive pattern
questions.exp: Schwannomatosis is a distinct genetic disorder caused by mutations in SMARCB1/INI1 or LZTR1 genes and is defined by multiple painful cranial, spinal, and peripheral schwannomas while strictly lacking bilateral vestibular schwannomas—the hallmark of NF2. Unlike classic NF2, patients with schwannomatosis typically have a normal lifespan but suffer from intractable neuropathic pain rather than hearing loss and neurologic morbidity. The absence of bilateral vestibular involvement and the SMARCB1 mutation confirm schwannomatosis rather than any NF2 subtype.
questions.source: Neurofibromatosis Type 2 (NF2 Gene, Merlin Protein, Bilateral Vestibular Schwannomas)

questions.q: In the context of soft-tissue filler injections in high-risk zones (glabella, nasolabial folds, nose), what is the primary medicolegal consequence of inadvertent intra-arterial injection that must be explicitly discussed in informed consent?
opts: Temporary erythema and edema lasting 2–3 weeks
Reversible tissue necrosis with full recovery after hyaluronidase administration
Irreversible blindness due to retrograde embolization into the central retinal artery
Mild nodule formation requiring manual massage
questions.exp: Inadvertent intra-arterial injection of fillers causes immediate ischemia and necrosis; when it involves retrograde embolization into the central retinal artery, it results in irreversible blindness—the most devastating and litigious complication of filler injection. This catastrophic risk must be explicitly discussed during informed consent, particularly in anatomically high-risk zones. The other options represent minor, reversible, or non-vision-threatening complications.

questions.q: A 32-year-old woman presents with bilaterally symmetrical, irregular brown patches over her cheeks, nose, forehead, and upper lip that worsened after starting oral contraceptives 6 months ago. Which of the following best describes the most likely distribution pattern of her condition?
opts: Malar pattern
Centrofacial pattern
Mandibular pattern
Extrafacial pattern
questions.exp: The patient's presentation with involvement of forehead, cheeks, nose, and upper lip (sparing the philtrum and nasolabial folds) is classic for the centrofacial distribution pattern, which is the most common pattern in melasma. The malar pattern would involve only cheeks and nose, while mandibular pattern affects the jawline.

questions.q: A researcher investigates how neutrophils contribute to skin antimicrobial defense. Which of the following proteins do neutrophils produce in their primary granules as part of the innate immune arsenal?
opts: Psoriasin and histone H4
Bactericidal/permeability-increasing protein (BPI) and defensins
Dermcidin and ribonucleases
LL-37 and calprotectin
questions.exp: Neutrophils produce bactericidal/permeability-increasing protein (BPI) and defensins stored in their primary granules, which are released upon activation to combat microbial pathogens. These represent critical components of neutrophil-mediated antimicrobial defense.

questions.q: A 3-year-old boy with a family history of tuberous sclerosis presents with multiple ash-leaf macules and focal seizures. Genetic testing identifies a TSC2 mutation inherited from his mother. Which statement best explains why TSC2 mutations typically produce a more severe clinical phenotype compared to TSC1 mutations?
opts: TSC2 encodes hamartin, which has direct inhibitory control over mTORC1 signaling
TSC2 encodes tuberin, a GTPase-activating protein that directly inhibits Rheb-GTP and suppresses mTORC1; loss of tuberin results in greater mTORC1 hyperactivation than hamartin loss
TSC2 mutations are exclusively autosomal recessive and therefore always manifest with higher penetrance
TSC2 is located on chromosome 9q34, whereas TSC1 is on 16p13.3, making TSC2 more susceptible to somatic second hits
questions.exp: The hamartin-tuberin heterodimer functions as a tumor suppressor complex. Tuberin (TSC2 product) is a GTPase-activating protein that directly converts Rheb-GTP to its inactive Rheb-GDP form, thereby suppressing mTORC1. Loss of tuberin removes this critical brake point, leading to greater constitutive mTORC1 activation and more severe hamartoma formation, intellectual disability, and treatment-resistant seizures. Hamartin (TSC1 product) acts as a cytoplasmic scaffold protein; its loss produces a comparatively milder phenotype.
questions.source: Tuberous Sclerosis Complex (TSC1 TSC2, Hamartin, Tuberin, Ash-Leaf, Shagreen, Koenen)

questions.q: A 28-year-old Brazilian patient with a history of cutaneous leishmaniasis 3 months ago (treated with topical therapy alone) now presents with nasal stuffiness and septal necrosis. What is the most critical management principle for preventing further mucocutaneous progression?
opts: Topical antifungal agents applied directly to nasal mucosa
Mandatory systemic treatment with pentavalent antimonials or intravenous Amphotericin B regardless of primary lesion size
Surgical debridement of necrotic tissue followed by observation
Intralesional corticosteroids to suppress local inflammation
questions.exp: Systemic treatment is always mandatory for any L. braziliensis infection because MCL does not self-heal and pursues a relentless, mutilating course. Inadequate or incomplete initial systemic treatment directly leads to relapse and mucosal metastasis. IV Amphotericin B is preferred for established or resistant MCL over pentavalent antimonials.
questions.hook: 🏰 Palace: The CASTLE GUARD (parasites) has already snuck PAST THE GATES once—you MUST deploy SYSTEMIC SOLDIERS (IV Amphotericin B) to patrol the ENTIRE KINGDOM, not just bandage the outer walls, or the enemy will march toward the THRONE (respiratory tract) and destroy everything.

questions.q: Which histopathological feature is considered pathognomonic for cylindroma and distinguishes it from other adnexal tumors?
opts: Single layer of cuboidal cells arranged in concentric rings
Basaloid cell nests arranged in a jigsaw puzzle pattern with a thick PAS-positive hyaline basement membrane cylinder
Dilated, keratinous-filled cystic structures lined by stratified squamous epithelium
Adipocytes intermixed with fibrous tissue in a honeycomb pattern
questions.exp: The distinctive jigsaw puzzle arrangement of basaloid cell nests combined with the thick, densely eosinophilic, PAS-positive (diastase-resistant) hyaline basement membrane sheath that surrounds individual tumor nests is virtually unmistakable and defines cylindroma histologically. This combination of architectural pattern and basement membrane morphology is the hallmark that makes cylindroma diagnosis straightforward on microscopy.

questions.q: A 35-year-old MSM patient presents with violaceous plaques on the lower extremities. Biopsy confirms Kaposi sarcoma with spindle cells expressing LYVE-1 and podoplanin. Which viral gene product is primarily responsible for converting blood vascular endothelial cells to a lymphatic endothelial phenotype through transcriptional reprogramming?
opts: LANA-1 (ORF 73) – maintains viral latency and inhibits apoptosis
vCyclin (ORF 72) – inhibits retinoblastoma protein to drive cell cycle progression
KSHV infection itself induces transcriptional changes in endothelial cells without a single gene product responsible
vGPCR (ORF 74) – constitutively activates inflammatory signaling pathways
questions.exp: Infection of blood vascular endothelial cells with KSHV induces transcriptional reprogramming that converts them toward a lymphatic endothelial phenotype, generating neoplastic spindle cells expressing lymphatic markers (LYVE-1, podoplanin, PROX1, VEGFR-3). This phenotypic switch is the result of the infection process itself rather than a single viral gene product.
questions.memory: 🏰 Palace: Imagine blood vessel cells in your castle being REPROGRAMMED into LYMPHATIC dancers (LYVE-1, podoplanin) by KSHV infection itself—the whole virus rewires their identity, not just one gene.

questions.q: A 28-year-old patient with atopic dermatitis shows elevated expression of psoriasin (S100A7). Based on the mechanisms described, which of the following best explains why psoriasin expression increases in this condition?
opts: Increased sebaceous gland activity
Enhanced TLR signaling from commensal bacteria
Skin barrier disruption and enhanced innate immune response
Elevated systemic levels of cathelicidins
questions.exp: Psoriasin (S100A7) expression is upregulated in atopic dermatitis and after skin barrier disruption as part of the adaptive innate immune response to restore barrier function and prevent infection. This represents the skin's attempt to compensate for compromised barrier integrity.

questions.q: Among infectious causes of balanitis documented in the literature, which organism was found in the highest percentage of balanoposthitis patients in a Swedish study?
opts: Candida albicans at 18%
Malassezia at 23%
Streptococcus species at 15%
Chlamydia trachomatis at 20%
questions.exp: A Swedish study documented Malassezia in 23% of balanoposthitis patients, making it the highest documented percentage in that population. While Candida albicans was found in 18% of patients in another study and is considered the commonest cause overall of infective balanitis, Malassezia showed higher prevalence in the Swedish cohort.
questions.mnemonic: 🏰 Palace: In the SWEDISH CASTLE, a SLIMY MALASSEZIA TROLL (23%) sits on the THRONE, beating the CANDIDA KNIGHT (18%) in the ranking—remember SWEDISH = MALASSEZIA WINS the numbers game.

questions.q: A 45-year-old woman presents with multiple pink to red nodules on her scalp that have gradually enlarged and coalesced over 20 years, forming a large mosaic plaque covering most of her head. Histopathology shows well-circumscribed dermal nodules with basaloid cells arranged in a jigsaw puzzle pattern, surrounded by a thick PAS-positive hyaline basement membrane. Which gene mutation is most likely responsible for this presentation?
opts: TP53 on chromosome 17p13
CYLD on chromosome 16q12-q13
BRCA1 on chromosome 17q21
NF1 on chromosome 17q11
questions.exp: The CYLD (cylindromatosis) tumor suppressor gene on chromosome 16q12-q13 is the key gene implicated in familial cylindromas and Brooke-Spiegler syndrome. Loss of CYLD function leads to uncontrolled NF-κB activation and unhindered cell proliferation. The presentation of multiple cylindromas with scalp involvement forming a 'turban tumor' is pathognomonic for CYLD-associated disease.

questions.q: A patient with suspected pemphigus vulgaris requires direct immunofluorescence (DIF) testing. What is the most critical error in specimen handling that would invalidate the DIF results?
opts: Taking the biopsy from the center of an intact blister rather than the edge
Placing the DIF specimen in formalin instead of Michel's medium or normal saline
Obtaining a shave biopsy instead of a punch biopsy
Failing to orient the specimen with a marker suture before fixation
questions.exp: Direct immunofluorescence specimens must NEVER be placed in formalin because formalin destroys the immunoglobulins required for diagnostic visualization on DIF. The specimen must be transported in Michel's medium, Zeus medium, or normal saline to preserve the antibody antigens at the basement membrane zone.

questions.q: A 28-year-old patient with newly diagnosed HIV infection and CD4 count <50 cells/μL develops Kaposi sarcoma. Which KSHV viral protein actively suppresses the host retinoblastoma (pRb) tumor suppressor, allowing cells to bypass G1 checkpoint and progress to S phase?
opts: vFLIP (ORF 71) – prevents apoptosis in latently infected cells
vCyclin (ORF 72) – viral cyclin D homolog that inactivates pRb
vGPCR (ORF 74) – activates PI3K-AKT-mTOR signaling cascade
vIL-6 – stimulates inflammatory response and B-cell proliferation
questions.exp: vCyclin (ORF 72) is a viral homolog of cellular cyclin D that directly inhibits the retinoblastoma tumor suppressor protein (pRb), allowing infected cells to bypass normal G1 arrest and progress into S phase, promoting uncontrolled proliferation. This is a classic mechanism of KSHV-driven oncogenic transformation.
questions.memory: 🏰 Palace: vCyclin (ORF 72) is a CLONE of cyclin D—imagine it SMASHING the retinoblastoma guardian at the G1 gate, forcing cells through like a BROKEN CHECKPOINT into S phase.

questions.q: During a dermatology case conference, a colleague asks which skin cell type is responsible for secreting dermcidin as part of the skin's antimicrobial defense. What is the correct answer?
opts: Keratinocytes
Sebocytes
Eccrine sweat gland epithelial cells
Langerhans cells
questions.exp: Dermcidin (DCD-1) is secreted by eccrine sweat gland epithelial cells and exhibits broad-spectrum antimicrobial activity. This secretion in sweat represents an important mechanism for protecting skin surfaces from microbial colonization.

questions.q: A dermatology clinic identifies a 5-year-old girl with unilateral facial angiofibromas strictly respecting the midline, confined to the right side of her face. Her parents are both phenotypically normal with negative genetic screening for TSC mutations. Systemic imaging reveals no renal angiomyolipomas, cardiac rhabdomyosarcomas, or brain hamartomas. What is the most likely genetic mechanism underlying her presentation?
opts: Autosomal dominant inheritance with incomplete penetrance in the parents
Postzygotic (somatic) TSC1 or TSC2 mutation during early embryogenesis resulting in segmental/mosaic TSC confined to the affected body region
TSC2/PKD1 contiguous gene deletion with mild systemic manifestations
NMI-TSC (No Mutation Identified) with intronic mutations detectable only by deep sequencing
questions.exp: Mosaic (segmental) TSC arises from a postzygotic somatic mutation in TSC1 or TSC2 during embryogenesis, affecting only the progenitor cells of a specific body segment. The characteristic finding is skin manifestations strictly localized to one region respecting the midline (as in this unilateral facial presentation) with absence of systemic complications such as renal or cardiac hamartomas. When the mutation remains isolated to the skin, systemic manifestations are absent; however, if gonadal tissue is involved, germline transmission of generalized TSC to offspring is possible.
questions.source: Tuberous Sclerosis Complex (TSC1 TSC2, Hamartin, Tuberin, Ash-Leaf, Shagreen, Koenen)

questions.q: According to Indian medical law standards for informed consent in cosmetic dermatology, which of the following is NOT a mandatory disclosure requirement to the patient?
opts: Nature of the ailment and proposed procedure
Pros and cons of the treatment
Alternative treatment options
The physician's personal financial incentives for recommending the procedure
questions.exp: Indian dermatology practice standards mandate disclosure of nature of ailment, proposed procedure, pros/cons, alternatives, substantial risks, and consequences of non-treatment. However, the physician's personal financial incentives are not listed as a mandatory disclosure requirement in the informed consent framework, though transparency about conflicts of interest is ethically important. The other three options are explicitly required disclosures under Indian medical law standards for valid informed consent.

questions.q: According to Linder's Scoring System for multibacillary (MB) leprosy relapse, which combination of factors would yield a score of ≥3 points, confirming the diagnosis of MB relapse?
opts: Initial BI ≥3+ (1 point), treatment completion 4 years ago (0 points), and average BI in current lesion 1+ higher than expected (0 points)
Treatment completion 65 months ago (3 points), initial BI ≥3+ (1 point), and absence of reaction signs (1 point) = 5 points
Treatment completion 50 months ago (0 points), initial BI <3+ (0 points), and BI in single lesion 3+ higher than expected (1 point)
Initial BI ≥3+ (1 point) and average BI 2+ higher than expected (1 point) with clinical presentation consistent with reaction signs (0 points)
questions.exp: Linder's Scoring System awards 3 points for time >60 months after treatment, 1 point for initial BI ≥3+, and 1 point each for BI in a single lesion ≥2+ higher than expected, average BI ≥2+ higher than expected, or absence of reaction signs. A total score of ≥3 diagnoses MB relapse. Option B achieves 5 points (3+1+1), exceeding the diagnostic threshold.

questions.q: A 42-year-old man with lepromatous leprosy completed adequate multidrug therapy (MDT) 7 years ago. He now presents with new skin lesions in previously unaffected areas and an increase in the bacteriological index (BI) of 3 log units compared to his baseline. On histopathology, active spindle-shaped macrophages packed with solid-staining AFB are noted. Which diagnostic criterion most strongly supports a diagnosis of relapse rather than reversal reaction?
opts: Appearance of new lesions and elevated BI, which will respond completely to systemic corticosteroids within 2–4 weeks
Presence of solid-staining (viable) bacilli on histopathology with increased BI of 2 or more log units, indicating multiplication of persister bacilli
Clinical presentation with new satellite lesions that feel like 'peas in a pod' and respond transiently to corticosteroid therapy
Reappearance of AFB in skin smears at a single anatomical site, confirming new infection rather than disease reactivation
questions.exp: True relapse in leprosy is caused by viable 'persister' bacilli multiplying after MDT completion. The solid-staining bacilli on histology and an increase in BI of ≥2 log units are hallmark bacteriological criteria for relapse. Unlike reversal reactions, relapse lesions will persist, enlarge, or show only partial improvement under corticosteroid cover. The presence of viable solid-staining bacilli strongly favors relapse over reaction.

questions.q: Which of the following pathophysiological mechanisms is considered the most significant trigger in the development of melasma?
opts: Increased number of melanocytes in lesional skin compared to perilesional skin
Ultraviolet radiation activating inducible nitric oxide and reactive oxygen species
Thyroid disease-induced hormonal dysregulation
Reduced expression of vascular endothelial growth factor by fibroblasts
questions.exp: UV radiation is the most significant trigger in melasma pathogenesis, activating inducible nitric oxide and reactive oxygen species (ROS) that promote melanogenesis. While hormonal factors and increased expression of growth factors like SCF, c-kit, and VEGF contribute to melasma, the number of melanocytes is typically similar between lesional and perilesional skin; those in affected areas are simply more biologically active.

questions.q: A 35-year-old man from Peru presents with a 2-year history of progressive nasal bridge collapse, epistaxis, and palatal perforation following a healed cutaneous ulcer on his cheek 4 years ago. Which immunopathological mechanism best explains the tissue destruction in mucocutaneous leishmaniasis (MCL)?
opts: T-cell anergy and tolerance allowing unrestricted parasite proliferation
Exaggerated Th1 hyperergic response with excessive pro-inflammatory cytokines causing host tissue destruction despite sparse parasites
Direct parasitic invasion overwhelming local immune defenses
IgE-mediated type I hypersensitivity reaction targeting mucosal epithelium
questions.exp: MCL pathogenesis is driven by a hyperergic Th1 response with massive TNF-alpha production that destroys host tissue in a futile attempt to clear sparse parasites. This is the pathophysiological opposite of DCL, which involves T-cell anergy. The exaggerated cellular immune response, not anergy or direct parasitic overwhelming, characterizes MCL's destructive course.
questions.hook: 🏰 Palace: Imagine a HYPERACTIVE BOUNCER (Th1) at the castle gate wildly swinging TNF-alpha baseball bats, smashing the ENTIRE CASTLE (host tissue) to kill one tiny invisible parasite hiding in the corner—the cure is worse than the disease.

questions.q: A 28-year-old uncircumcised male presents to the GUM clinic with inflammation affecting both the glans penis and the prepuce. Which of the following statements about his condition is correct?
opts: Balanoposthitis can occur in both circumcised and uncircumcised males with equal frequency
By definition, balanoposthitis does not occur in circumcised males
Posthitis alone is sufficient to diagnose balanoposthitis
Balanitis and balanoposthitis are synonymous terms with identical clinical presentations
questions.exp: Balanoposthitis is defined as inflammation of both the glans penis and the mucosal surface of the prepuce, and by definition cannot occur in circumcised males who lack a prepuce. Balanitis refers only to glans inflammation, while posthitis refers only to preputial inflammation; balanoposthitis requires both to be present.
questions.mnemonic: 🏰 Palace: Picture a CIRCUMCISED KNIGHT who has had his castle DRAWBRIDGE (prepuce) removed—he cannot have BALANO-POSTHITIS (both parts inflamed) because one part is GONE. Only the uncircumcised knight with both glans AND foreskin can suffer the full 'BOTH-PART' inflammation.

questions.q: A 28-year-old patient presents with bilateral hearing loss and is found to have bilateral vestibular schwannomas on MRI. Genetic testing reveals a nonsense mutation in the NF2 gene on chromosome 22q12. Which of the following best explains why this truncating mutation typically results in a more severe clinical phenotype?
opts: It produces a partially functional but unstable merlin protein that retains some tumor-suppressor activity
It completely abolishes merlin protein production, eliminating all contact inhibition and Hippo pathway regulation
It causes overexpression of the ERM protein family, leading to excessive cell proliferation
It triggers an autoimmune response against neuroectodermal cells via HLA-associated pathways
questions.exp: Truncating mutations (nonsense, frameshift) in NF2 completely abolish merlin protein production, representing the most severe loss-of-function type and are associated with the Wishart (early-onset, severe) phenotype. This patient's presentation with bilateral vestibular schwannomas before age 30 and a truncating mutation is consistent with Wishart-type NF2. Merlin is the critical tumor suppressor of the ERM family that regulates contact inhibition and the Hippo signaling pathway; its complete absence eliminates these protective mechanisms.
questions.source: Neurofibromatosis Type 2 (NF2 Gene, Merlin Protein, Bilateral Vestibular Schwannomas)

questions.q: A 45-year-old man with serological evidence of active hepatitis B infection presents with constitutional symptoms, peripheral neuropathy, and angiographic findings of microaneurysms in mesenteric vessels. What is the proposed immunopathological mechanism driving vasculitis in this clinical scenario?
opts: Direct viral invasion of vascular endothelial cells with intranuclear viral inclusions
Formation and deposition of immune complexes containing hepatitis B surface antigen (HBsAg) and immunoglobulins
ANCA-mediated neutrophil activation and degranulation within the vessel wall
Complement-independent antibody-mediated Type II hypersensitivity targeting basement membranes
questions.exp: In hepatitis B-associated PAN, the pathophysiology is driven by immune complex-mediated vascular damage, specifically through the formation and deposition of immune complexes containing hepatitis B surface antigen (HBsAg) and corresponding immunoglobulins. This represents the central mechanism of medium-vessel vasculitis in HBV-associated disease, which historically accounted for up to 30% of classic PAN cases.

questions.q: According to the revised International Chapel Hill Consensus Conference nomenclature, which of the following findings would EXCLUDE a diagnosis of polyarteritis nodosa (PAN)?
opts: Necrotizing vasculitis of medium-sized muscular arteries at bifurcations
Presence of glomerulonephritis on renal biopsy
Absence of ANCA antibodies
Formation of microaneurysms and vessel wall weakening
questions.exp: PAN is definitively classified as a medium-vessel vasculitis with the strict absence of glomerulonephritis and lack of vasculitis in arterioles, capillaries, or venules. The presence of glomerulonephritis would argue against PAN and suggest an alternative diagnosis such as microscopic polyangiitis (MPA) or granulomatosis with polyangiitis (GPA). ANCA negativity is a hallmark of PAN that distinguishes it from these other vasculitides.

questions.q: A 42-year-old immunocompromised patient develops recurrent skin infections. Understanding AMP mechanisms, which structural feature enables most cationic AMPs to selectively disrupt bacterial membranes while preserving host cell membranes?
opts: Hydrophobic interaction with lipid bilayers
Electrostatic interaction with negatively charged bacterial membrane surfaces
Competitive inhibition of membrane proteins
Enzymatic degradation of peptidoglycan
questions.exp: Cationic AMPs interact with the negatively charged surfaces of bacterial membranes through electrostatic interactions, leading to membrane disruption. This charge-based selectivity explains their preferential activity against bacteria while minimizing damage to host cell membranes, which are typically less negatively charged.
